So the question is: how many health impacts would have been avoided had the exempt plants saw their pollution increase at the rate of the non-exempt plants?

It would have prevented 359-667 deaths & $5.5-10B in damages. An ~70% reduction in health costs.

The 145 plants seeking exemptions saw NOx, SO2, & CO2 jump by 14.5%, 22.6, and 12.6%, respectively. The NOx and SO2 increases were far higher than the 12.7% increase in MWh.

There were 164 instances in which NOx or SO2 emissions rose by more than MWh. 3/4 of these were at plants seeking exemptions.

The 64 plants that did not seek a MATS exemption saw their NOx, SO2, and CO2 emissions increase 6%, 2.8%, and 5.7%, respectively.

These increases were all less than the 6.6% increase in power output from those plants.

While the 209 plants increased their power output by 11.6% to 813.5 TWh from 729.1 TWh, pollution increased more.

NOx rose by 12.8%, and SO2 rose by 18.6%. CO2 was in line with output, rising by 11.3%.

But this does not tell us about the impact of the 2-year MATS exemptions. So let's hone in.

We already know that coal-fired power generation increased in 2025, as increasing natural gas prices led to a rise in demand for coal. But was the change in air pollution proportional to the increase in electricity output?

In a word, no.
